items.text: The system shall permit Autopilot operation only within a validated operational design domain and shall inhibit activation or alert the driver when road, visibility, or traffic conditions are outside that domain.
The system shall assess driver attention and readiness to take control using evidence beyond steering-wheel torque, and shall not treat hands on the wheel alone as proof of attentiveness.
The system shall provide timely, escalating takeover alerts when the driver must resume control and shall transition to a defined safe state if the driver does not respond.
The system shall detect vehicles crossing or entering the vehicle’s path and shall warn or intervene when a collision is imminent.
The system shall use lane-boundary confidence to determine whether Autosteer can operate safely, and shall alert the driver and limit or disengage steering assistance when lane guidance is uncertain.
The system shall maintain a safe speed and following distance appropriate to detected traffic, road geometry, visibility, and available braking capability.
The system shall detect sensor, processing, or actuator faults and degraded performance, notify the driver, and prevent continued operation when safe control cannot be assured.
The system shall clearly indicate when each automation feature is active, what control it is providing, and when it engages, disengages, or changes capability.

The system shall provide collision warnings and automatic emergency braking when a detected hazard presents an imminent collision risk, including hazards the driving automation may not otherwise respond to.
The system shall allow the driver to override automation promptly and shall make transfers between automated and manual control predictable and stable.

You are a requirements engineer reviewing a safety-critical system.

things the system should do or guarantee for safe operation that the description does not cover.
Give at most 10, ranked from most to least important.

System description:
# Case: Tesla Model S with Autopilot (Williston, Florida, 2016)

Source: NTSB Highway Accident Report HAR-17/02. This is a description of the system and its use before the crash. It does not include the investigation findings.

## System
A 2015 Tesla Model S has Autopilot, a SAE Level 2 partial driving automation feature. It combines Traffic-Aware Cruise Control (TACC) and Autosteer (lane keeping). The driver stays responsible for driving and monitoring the road.

## Main parts
- Sensors: a forward-facing camera, a forward-facing radar and ultrasonic sensors.
- Vision processing: a camera-based system detects lane markings and objects ahead.
- TACC: holds a speed set by the driver, slows down for a vehicle ahead in the same lane, and speeds up again when the lane is clear.
- Autosteer: keeps the vehicle centered in its lane using lane markings and the vehicle ahead.
- Forward collision warning and automatic emergency braking are available as separate features.
- Driver monitoring: the system checks that the driver's hands are on the steering wheel by sensing steering torque, and shows visual and audible alerts if no hands are detected for a period of time.

## People
- The driver sets the cruising speed, turns Autopilot on, and is told to keep hands on the wheel and watch the road.
- Other road users include cars, large trucks crossing or joining the road, and motorcyclists.

## Operating context
Autopilot is intended mainly for highways with limited access, in good visibility. Drivers can also turn it on for other roads, such as divided highways with cross traffic at intersections.
